title: No Good Outcomes For Energy Inflation
text:
No Good Outcomes For Energy Inflation

Tom Holland

Gavekal Research | 9 Sep 2026

It is Wednesday. The US and Iran are exchanging fire in the Middle East. So are Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement. And energy prices are spiking, with the price of the Brent crude oil benchmark trading as high as US$99.68/bbl in Asian hours. For investors, it may be tempting to shrug off the latest flare-up in Middle Eastern fighting; everyone has heard this tune repeatedly in recent months, and the world did not end. On the contrary, stock markets in the US and elsewhere defied the drum-beat of war to set new highs over the summer. Yet disregarding the latest escalation in the Persian Gulf would be rash; developments in the region will matter greatly for the trajectory of inflation over the coming months, and therefore for financial markets.Historically, inflation—and inflation expectations—have tended to march in lockstep with benchmark energy prices, which is pretty much what you would expect given the Gavekal dictum that “the economy is just energy transformed.” This relationship implies that US CPI data will show an uptick in inflation into September (the figures for August will be published on Friday; the consensus is for no change).
